extracted.intended_audience: university mathematics instructors, course designers, and assessment practitioners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and criteria for designing, running, and evaluating assessment practices in undergraduate mathematics courses (early student feedback sessions, topic letters, and course portfolios). Includes procedural steps, goals, evidence types, and success factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Goal: Establish constructive student attitudes
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish constructive student attitudes about the value of mathematics by highlighting its link to the real world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the explicit educational objectives to guide course design and assessment in introductory calculus; used to frame feedback and adjustments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Goal: Persuade students to continue in math/science
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuade more students to continue in subsequent mathematics and science courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A program-level aim that should influence course activities and be measurable via student choices and attitudes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Goal: Increase faculty commitment and contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Increase faculty commitment to the course by increasing the amount of student-faculty contact during each class period and having faculty grade students' homework themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Operational goal affecting staffing, grading policies, and classroom interactions; assessable through observation and feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Goal: Develop wide base of calculus knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Develop a wide base of calculus knowledge including: basic skills, understanding of concepts, geometric visualization, and the thought processes of problem-solving, predicting, and generalizing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a variety of assessments (skills, conceptual, visualization, problem-solving) to measure progress toward this multidimensional goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Goal: Strengthen general academic skills
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen students' general academic skills such as: critical thinking, writing, giving clear verbal explanations, understanding and using technology, and working collaboratively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include assignments and assessments that explicitly require these skills (e.g., essays, presentations, group work).

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Goal: Improve quantitative reasoning and judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Improve students' ability to give reasonable descriptions and to form valid judgments based on quantitative information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design tasks that require interpretation of quantitative results and justification of conclusions; use feedback to monitor growth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Feature: Emphasize underlying concepts and real-world problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Course content: The course emphasizes the underlying concepts and incorporate challenging real-world problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer conceptual framing and application problems over purely procedural exercises; use these to assess transfer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Feature: Textbook use across multiple representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Textbook: The textbook emphasizes the need to understand problems numerically, graphically, and through English descriptions as well as by the traditional algebraic approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage multi-representational understanding; design assignments that require numerical, graphical, and verbal explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Feature: Cooperative learning classroom atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: Classroom atmosphere: The classroom environment uses cooperative learning and promotes experimentation by students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure activities for small-group collaboration and risk-taking; assess through observation and student feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Feature: Team homework assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Team homework assignments: A significant portion of each student's grade is based on solutions to interesting problems submitted jointly with a team of three other students and graded by the instructors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use group tasks graded for understanding and process; monitor group logistics and workload uniformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Feature: Use of technology (graphing calculators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Technology: Graphing calculators are used throughout the introductory courses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Integrate technology into assignments and assess students' appropriate use and understanding of technological outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Key Feature: Student responsibility for reading and writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Student responsibility: Students are required to read the textbook, discuss the problems with other students, and write full essay answers to most exercises.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make reading and written explanation routine parts of assessment; check notebooks or assignments periodically for effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Timing and basic procedure
rubrics_metrics.description: Approximately one-third of the way into the term, each class is visited by an instructional consultant who observes class until ~20 minutes remain, the instructor leaves, and the consultant runs a feedback session; consultant and instructor later debrief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Run while course is in progress so adjustments can be made; keep sessions confidential and structured.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Consultant selection and training
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultants are the instructors who run the professional development program (upper-level graduate students and faculty) and are trained according to CRLT guidelines for observing classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure consultants are trained to have instructors reflect on plans/goals for each session and to observe objectively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Observational protocol
rubrics_metrics.description: During the observation period, the consultant objectively records everything as it happens: classroom setup, what the instructor says and does, student interactions with the instructor and each other, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record concrete behaviors and context to provide factual backup during debrief; avoid evaluative language in notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Small-group consensus feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: In the feedback session, the class is divided into small groups (4–5), given 7 minutes to discuss and reach consensus, and to record responses on the Early Feedback Form focusing on 'Strengths' and 'Changes'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask groups to use detailed examples and specific suggestions; have a recorder write agreed comments; consultant elicits one item at a time from groups and records on the board in students' own words while checking for clarity and consensus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Feedback Form: Strengths and Changes categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Early Feedback Form prompts: List the major strengths in this course (what is helping you learn) — up to five responses; List changes that could be made in the course to assist your learning — up to five responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly structure feedback into 'strengths' (start) and 'changes' (follow); provide space limits to keep comments focused.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Debriefing the instructor
rubrics_metrics.description: Consultant prepares a two-page list (strengths one page, changes the other), begins debrief by eliciting instructor reflection on goals/strengths/weaknesses, then goes over student comments point-by-point, using observations as backup, and plans responses/adjustments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discuss which student requests can/cannot be accommodated and why (e.g., explain pedagogical rationale if declining a request), and plan messaging back to students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Confidentiality of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Early Student Feedback session is confidential and the results are never recorded on an individual instructor's record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confidentiality to make process less threatening and encourage open student discussion; consultants may still look for course-level patterns across sessions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Feedback: Course-profile questions
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask course-level questions when analyzing results: Do students see the value of homework teams? Is there lots of interaction? Are students involved? Are instructors spending too much time on their teaching?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these diagnostic questions to form a clear profile and to decide timely adjustments to instruction and course design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Cost/time estimate and efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Time costs: Students – 20 minutes of class time; Instructors – 1/2 to 1 hour debriefing; Consultants – 1 hour class visit + 1 hour preparation + 1/2–1 hour debriefing. Method is cheap compared to information generated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the low time/cost to justify routine implementation; plan consultant workload accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Early Student Feedback: Success factor — mandatory routine
rubrics_metrics.description: Making the process mandatory every term in every section had the effect of making it seem like a routine (and hence less threatening) part of each term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider institutionalizing the practice to normalize it and create experienced consultants and instructors who will promote it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Letters: Audience requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must write the topic letter to someone who has never studied the mathematics in question but has the same working knowledge they had at the start of the course.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Setting this audience forces students to explain concepts clearly and focus on 'big picture' understanding rather than using jargon to impress the instructor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Letters: Primary grading criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are graded based primarily on the insight and mathematical correctness displayed; quality of insight (not quantity of facts) is the key feature of a strong letter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize conceptual clarity and correctness; provide written suggestions to students who submit weak letters and allow revisions (except for end-of-semester letters).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Letters: Format and length guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: To allow freedom in expression, do not set page limits or rigid formatting; most letters fall into the 3–5 typed page range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell students to write 'no more or less than is needed' to convey ideas clearly; avoid over-prescribing format to preserve voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Letters: Revision policy and feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: Students who submit weak topic letters are encouraged to revise them and the instructor provides specific written suggestions; end-of-semester letters collected in last week are not permitted revisions but are given full credit if a serious effort was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use iterative feedback to improve conceptual writing; balance instructor time with the educational benefit (reading takes ~10–15 minutes per letter).

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Letters: Using letters as course evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Topic letters provide information about student conceptual understanding and about how well the instructor designed experiences for conceptual insight; watch for signs that the course overemphasized mechanics (letters with examples/algorithms but no concepts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze collections of letters (not just individuals) to get a course-level reading; use letters to inform changes in assessment (e.g., replace mechanics quizzes with conceptual take-home quizzes) and instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Topic Letters: Non-anonymity and validity concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are not anonymous which may limit their validity as course evaluation tools; some students may aim for shock value or write emotionally charged letters if they did poorly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sort mathematical/course information from provocative content; be prepared to handle emotionally difficult letters sensitively and use them as authentic feedback about discouraging experiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Start with syllabus and explicit goals
rubrics_metrics.description: The course portfolio starts with the course syllabus, with explicit mathematical goals for students in the course; prerequisites, goals, and the course information sheet become portfolio elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make goals explicit and distribute them to students; use the syllabus as the organizing spine for the portfolio.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Include background knowledge probe and item analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a pre-course background knowledge probe testing prerequisite skills and course goals; include the probe and an item analysis in the portfolio to compare with final exam scores as a measure of student learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design probe items representative of final-exam-style tasks; use item analysis to document learning gains.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Collect diverse evidence of student learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Include homework assignments, copies of exams, projects, minute papers, in-class assessments, solutions, scores, and a collated 'student voice' (informal and formal evaluations) as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample performance selectively (don't amass everything); include multiple kinds of evidence to show the argument that learning occurred.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Include course reflection memo
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a 'course reflection memo' at the end of the course addressing appropriateness of goals, student progress, problems, and recommendations; place it near the front of the portfolio.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflective commentary to reveal pedagogical thinking and to guide readers' interpretation of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Portfolio as argument organized around goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of the portfolio as an argument, a case, a thesis with relevant evidence and examples cited; organize the portfolio around goals (your own or departmental).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be selective in evidence; provide reflective commentary explaining why included items support claims about teaching and learning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: AAHE success factors (seek agreement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Seek agreement at the outset about the purposes of portfolios, who will use the information, who owns it, and what's at stake.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clarify expectations with peers or reviewers before assembling the portfolio to avoid misunderstandings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: AAHE success factors (be selective)
rubrics_metrics.description: Be selective. The power of the portfolio comes from sampling performance, not amassing every possible scrap of information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose representative artifacts that align with stated goals; avoid overwhelming readers with unnecessary material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: AAHE success factors (include variety and reflective commentary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a variety of kinds of evidence from a variety of sources and provide reflective commentary on evidence to reveal pedagogical thinking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reflective notes to orient readers to what to look for and how pieces of evidence support claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Experimentation and focused portfolio variant
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiment with various formats and structures; consider a 'focused portfolio' which concentrates on one specific aspect or goal of the course (e.g., calculator integration or transition to proof-creating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be deliberate about format and whether portfolios are working; a focused portfolio can be shorter and target a specific stake or review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Use for peer review and transfer to other instructors
rubrics_metrics.description: A course portfolio provides a platform for peer feedback, professional accountability, and can be passed to other instructors to inform coverage, pace, and standards.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the portfolio to support peer review of teaching and to help new or replacement instructors adopt course structure and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Course Portfolio: Time expectation
rubrics_metrics.description: Preparing a course portfolio requires time; estimated about an average of one hour per week through the term, with more effort at the beginning (goals/organization) and end (assessment/reflection) of the term.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan portfolio work across the term to make it manageable; keep collection of artifacts routine and automatic during the course.
